a: Asking a database for records, and adding, changing or deleting them
tasks.fb: SQL is the language databases understand.

tasks.q: Which part of a website would use SQL?
a: The login page checking a username and password
tasks.fb: Any page that looks up stored data uses queries like this.

tasks.q: Joining a string to a variable, as in 'uname = ' + username, is known as what?
tasks.fb: This is the answer to your starter question.

tasks.q: Why is building a query this way dangerous?
a: Anything the user types becomes part of the SQL command
It makes the website load slowly
tasks.fb: The database can't tell the difference between the programmer's code and the user's input.

tasks.q: What does ' OR 1=1 do inside a query?
a: It makes the condition always true, so every record matches
tasks.fb: 1=1 is always true, so the WHERE clause stops filtering anything.

a: It turns the rest of the line into a comment, so it is ignored
tasks.fb: Commenting out the rest removes anything that would break the attacker's query.

tasks.q: What can a successful SQL injection attack achieve? Select all that apply.
opts: Bypass a login and enter as another user
Read personal data from the database
correct: Bypass a login and enter as another user
Read personal data from the database
tasks.fb: The attacker gets whatever access the website's database account has.

tasks.q: Which is the strongest defence against SQL injection?
a: Using parameterised queries, so input is never treated as code
tasks.fb: Validation and sanitisation help, but parameterised queries remove the problem.

a: Removing or escaping characters that could change the meaning of the query
tasks.fb: For example, escaping a single quotation mark so it is treated as text.

tasks.q: Why do companies pay penetration testers?
a: To find weaknesses like SQL injection before criminals do
tasks.fb: It's legal because the company gives permission.

tasks.q: Why hide detailed error messages on a live site?
a: They can tell an attacker how the database is built
tasks.fb: Error messages are useful to developers, and just as useful to attackers.

tasks.q: Is each practice safe or risky when writing a login page?
items: Building the query by joining text to the user's input
Checking input contains only letters and numbers
Showing the full database error on the page
Giving the website's database account full admin rights
Removing or escaping quotation marks in input
Trusting that users will only type a username
tasks.fb: Never trust input from a user: that's the lesson behind every one of these.

info.title: Little Bobby Tables
info.text: A famous web comic shows a pupil named 'Robert'); DROP TABLE Students;--' whose name deletes a school's database. It's a joke, but the attack is real.

info.title: Still in the top ten
info.text: Injection attacks have been in the OWASP list of the ten most serious web security risks for over 20 years.

info.title: TalkTalk
info.text: In 2015, a UK telecoms company was fined £400,000 after an SQL injection attack exposed the details of around 157,000 customers.

info.title: It's not just logins
info.text: Search boxes, contact forms and even web addresses can all be injection points if the input isn't handled safely.

info.title: Hashing passwords
info.text: Even if attackers steal a database, properly hashed passwords are extremely hard to reverse. Storing plain-text passwords is a serious mistake.

info.title: Automated scanners
info.text: Attackers use automated tools that test thousands of sites for injection flaws, so even small websites are targets.
